# Introduction

A Forest plot of the same covariate, drawn from an SCM model and from a FREM
model of the same data, can point in opposite directions without either being
wrong. They answer different questions, and the difference is not in the
estimation but in two choices made when the plot is drawn: what the predictions
are conditioned on, and what they are compared against.

This vignette shows which question each plot answers, and how to make one FREM
model produce either.

# 1. Conditional and unconditional covariate effects

**A conditional covariate effect** is the isolated effect of one covariate with
every other covariate held fixed. It supports a mechanistic reading - what this
covariate does, once the others are accounted for - and it requires a
multivariable model.

**An unconditional covariate effect** is the total effect of a covariate,
whatever else it travels with in the population. It supports label statements
and dosing recommendations - what to expect of a subject known only by this one
covariate - and it is what a univariable model estimates.

An SCM produces one multivariable model, so its Forest plot is conditional. FREM
estimates the covariates jointly and can be reduced to any subset of them, so a
single FREM model can answer either question. Which one it answers depends on
how the plot is set up.

# 2. What the two defaults do

|  | SCM | FREM (default) |
|---|---|---|
| Predictions | conditional on all other covariates | unconditional |
| Reference | a typical subject as the model is parameterised - centred on the median, or the most common category | a typical subject as the *data* defines it: the mean predicted parameter value across the covariates |

Neither default is the "right" one. They differ because the two methods were
built for different readings, which is why the same covariate can sit on
opposite sides of 1 in the two plots.

# 3. The two controls

Everything below is done with two inputs, and both are built by PMXForest rather
than assembled by hand:

* **`dfCovs`**, from `setupDfCovs()` - one row per Forest plot row. The
  covariates active in a row are the ones the prediction is conditioned on. With
  `useMissVal = TRUE` (the default) every other covariate is left at `missVal`
  and only one is active per row; with `useMissVal = FALSE` the inactive ones
  are set to their reference value instead, which conditions every row on them.
* **`dfRefRow`**, from `setupDfRefRow()` - the covariate values the predictions
  are compared against. `singleRef = TRUE` returns one row, and that same
  comparator is used by every row of the plot. `singleRef = FALSE` returns a
  data frame with as many rows as `dfCovs`, so each row of the plot gets its own
  comparator. Passing no `dfRefRow` at all leaves the FREM default in place.

Both take `contRef` and `catRef` to say what "reference" means for each
covariate - a number, `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"mode"`, `"lowest"`, or `"model"`
to read it from the control stream. The defaults are the median of a continuous
covariate and the most common level of a categorical one.

The other choice is the scale: `plotRelative = TRUE` plots each row as a ratio
to its reference, `FALSE` on the parameter's own scale.

# 4. Setup

```{r setup}
library(PMXFrem)
library(PMXForest)
library(ggplot2)
library(data.table)

set.seed(865765)
theme_set(theme_bw(base_size = 14))

modDevDir <- system.file("extdata/SimNeb", package = "PMXFrem")
fremFiles <- getFileNames(modName = "run31", modDevDir = modDevDir)

data <- fread(
  file.path(modDevDir, "DAT-2-MI-PMX-2-onlyTYPE2-new.csv"),
  data.table = FALSE
)

covariates <- c("AGE", "GENO2", "RACEL", "WT")
```

Four covariates are enough to make the point, and keep the plots readable:

```{r dfcovs}
dfCovs <- setupDfCovs(
  data       = data,
  covariates = covariates,
  probs      = c(0.05, 0.9),
  idVar      = "ID",
  missVal    = -99
)

dfCovs
```

Each row sets one covariate and leaves the rest at `missVal`. What that means
depends on the model behind the parameter function. In a **FREM** model the
covariates left at `missVal` are integrated out, so the prediction is
unconditional. In an **SCM** or FFEM parameter function there is nothing to
integrate over: `missVal` triggers the model's own missing-covariate handling,
which puts the covariate at its reference - so the prediction is conditioned on
the reference values rather than unconditional. Same `dfCovs`, two different
readings, which is where the two plots start to diverge.

```{r samples}
dfExt <- subset(getExt(extFile = fremFiles$ext), ITERATION == "-1000000000")

dfParameters <- getSamples(fremFiles$cov, extFile = fremFiles$ext, n = 100)
dfParameters[1, ] <- dfExt[1, -1] # first sample = the final estimates

# CL is THETA(2) in run31, and the model's first FREM parameter
functionList <- list(
  function(basethetas, covthetas, ...) basethetas[2] * exp(covthetas[1])
)
```

`RACEL` is coded 1 Caucasian, 2 Black and 3 Other, with level 1 as the
reference, so the one-hot columns `RACEL_2` and `RACEL_3` carry the other two.

For didactic purposes in this vignette, the default labels are kept in full. The
varying dimensions of the resulting plots are managed through the small wrapper
function below.

```{r plot_helper}
fp <- function(dfres, left = 30, relative = TRUE, ...) {
  forestPlot(dfres,
    parameters = "CL", plotRelative = relative,
    errbartabwidth = c(3, 1), ...
  ) +
    theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 5.5, 5.5, left))
}
```

# 5. The FREM default: unconditional

```{r default}
dfres_default <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovs,
  runno            = 31,
  modDevDir        = modDevDir,
  dfParameters     = dfParameters,
  functionList     = functionList,
  functionListName = "CL",
  quiet            = TRUE
)

data.frame(
  row       = dfres_default$COVNAME,
  CL        = round(dfres_default$POINT, 3),
  reference = round(dfres_default$REFFUNC, 3),
  relative  = round(dfres_default$POINT / dfres_default$REFFUNC, 3)
)
```

The same reference value for every row, and each row varies one covariate only.

```{r default_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
fp(dfres_default)
```

# 6. Moving the reference

The reference need not be the one FREM computes from the data.
`setupDfRefRow()` builds one from the covariates themselves - here the typical
subject an SCM model would be centred on, the median of each continuous
covariate and the most common level of each categorical one:

```{r ref_single}
dfRefRow <- setupDfRefRow(
  dfCovs     = dfCovs,
  data       = data,
  covariates = covariates,
  singleRef  = TRUE
)

dfRefRow

dfres_typRef <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovs,
  runno            = 31,
  modDevDir        = modDevDir,
  dfParameters     = dfParameters,
  functionList     = functionList,
  functionListName = "CL",
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRow,
  quiet            = TRUE
)

c(default = dfres_default$REFFUNC[1], typical = dfres_typRef$REFFUNC[1])
```

Every point estimate is unchanged - only what they are divided by has moved, so
the whole plot shifts. The predictions are still unconditional.

```{r ref_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
fp(dfres_typRef,
  referenceInfo = "Reference: the typical subject - median AGE and WT, most common GENO2 and RACEL"
)
```

## A reference subject at another level of a categorical covariate

The most common level of `RACEL` is level 1. Level 1 is also the level that is
left out of the indicator columns of the FREM model, `RACEL_2` and `RACEL_3`.
A reference subject at another level, here level 2 (Black), is built with
`catRef` in `setupDfCovs()`. `setupDfCovs()` records `catRef` in an attribute
of `dfCovs`, and `setupDfRefRow()` reads it from there, so `catRef` is given
once:

```{r ref_level}
dfCovsBlack <- setupDfCovs(
  data       = data,
  covariates = covariates,
  probs      = c(0.05, 0.9),
  idVar      = "ID",
  missVal    = -99,
  catRef     = list(RACEL = 2)
)

dfRefRowBlack <- setupDfRefRow(
  dfCovs     = dfCovsBlack,
  data       = data,
  covariates = covariates,
  singleRef  = TRUE
)

dfRefRowBlack
```

In `dfCovsBlack` and `dfRefRowBlack`, the indicator columns are `RACEL_1` and
`RACEL_3`: level 2 is left out, and a row of zeros is level 2. The model has
`RACEL_2` and `RACEL_3`. `getForestDFFREM()` recodes the columns of `dfCovs`
and `dfRefRow` to the columns of the model, and every row describes the same
subject after the recoding: the reference row, a row of zeros before, has
`RACEL_2 = 1` and `RACEL_3 = 0` after. With `quiet = FALSE`,
`getForestDFFREM()` prints a message with the recoded columns.

```{r ref_level_df}
dfres_blackRef <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovsBlack,
  runno            = 31,
  modDevDir        = modDevDir,
  dfParameters     = dfParameters,
  functionList     = functionList,
  functionListName = "CL",
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRowBlack,
  quiet            = TRUE
)
```

The rows of `dfCovsBlack` describe the same subjects as the rows of `dfCovs`,
so the point estimates are those of the plot with the typical subject as the
reference. Only the reference has moved, from level 1 to level 2 of `RACEL`:

```{r ref_level_check}
all.equal(dfres_blackRef$POINT, dfres_typRef$POINT)

c(level1 = dfres_typRef$REFFUNC[1], level2 = dfres_blackRef$REFFUNC[1])
```

```{r ref_level_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
fp(dfres_blackRef,
  referenceInfo = "Reference: median AGE and WT, most common GENO2, RACEL level 2 (Black)"
)
```

In PMXFrem 2.4.0 and earlier, the indicator columns were not recoded. A
reference subject at level 2 then needed a `dfCovs` and a `dfRefRow` in the
coding of the model, with `RACEL_2 = 1` written by hand into `dfRefRow` and,
with `useMissVal = FALSE`, into every row of `dfCovs` that does not vary
`RACEL`.

# 7. Conditioning the predictions: mimicking SCM

To read the plot the way an SCM plot is read, the predictions have to be
conditioned as well. That is `useMissVal = FALSE`: the covariates a row is not
varying are set to their reference instead of to `missVal`.

```{r scm_like}
dfCovsCond <- setupDfCovs(
  data        = data,
  covariates  = covariates,
  probs       = c(0.05, 0.9),
  idVar       = "ID",
  missVal     = -99,
  useMissVal  = FALSE
)

dfCovsCond

dfres_scm <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovsCond,
  runno            = 31,
  modDevDir        = modDevDir,
  dfParameters     = dfParameters,
  functionList     = functionList,
  functionListName = "CL",
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRow,
  quiet            = TRUE
)

data.frame(
  row          = dfres_scm$COVNAME,
  relative_SCM = round(dfres_scm$POINT / dfres_scm$REFFUNC, 3)
)
```

Every row now carries every covariate, and the reference is that same typical
subject - which is what an SCM Forest plot shows. This is also visible in the
y-axis labels, kept here at their default: each covariate value that is not
`missVal` is included in the label.

```{r scm_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
# the conditioned labels are long, so this one needs a wider margin
fp(dfres_scm,
  left = 95,
  referenceInfo = "Reference: the typical subject, with every prediction conditioned on it"
)
```

# 8. A reference that varies by covariate group

The unconditional reading is sharper when each covariate is compared against its
own reference rather than against one subject. That is `singleRef = FALSE`,
which returns a reference row per row of `dfCovs`:

```{r var_ref}
dfRefRowVarying <- setupDfRefRow(
  dfCovs     = dfCovs,
  data       = data,
  covariates = covariates,
  singleRef  = FALSE
)

dfRefRowVarying

dfres_varRef <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovs,
  runno            = 31,
  modDevDir        = modDevDir,
  dfParameters     = dfParameters,
  functionList     = functionList,
  functionListName = "CL",
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRowVarying,
  quiet            = TRUE
)

data.frame(
  row       = dfres_varRef$COVNAME,
  reference = round(dfres_varRef$REFFUNC, 3),
  relative  = round(dfres_varRef$POINT / dfres_varRef$REFFUNC, 3)
)
```

Each covariate group now sits at 1 for its own reference level:

```{r var_ref_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
fp(dfres_varRef,
  referenceInfo = "Reference varies by covariate: the median or most common level of each"
)
```

On the relative scale the varying reference is invisible - every group is
divided by its own value, so every group has a line at 1. On the absolute scale
it can be seen: the reference moves between covariate groups.

```{r var_ref_abs, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5, out.width = "100%"}
fp(dfres_varRef,
  relative = FALSE,
  referenceInfo = "Reference varies by covariate: the median or most common level of each"
)
```

# 9. Which plot answers which question

The two readings can disagree, and on this model they do. Take the subjects of
`RACEL` level 3, Other:

```{r estimands}
# the dfCovs row for RACEL level 3. Match on the row number rather than
# the label: conditioning rewrites the label to carry every covariate it fixes.
iRacel3 <- which(dfCovs$COVARIATEGROUPS == "RACEL" & dfCovs$RACEL_3 == 1)

pick <- function(d) {
  r <- d[d$COVNUM == iRacel3, ]
  round(r$POINT / r$REFFUNC, 3)
}

c(unconditional = pick(dfres_varRef), conditional = pick(dfres_scm))
```

* **Unconditional**, `r pick(dfres_varRef)` of the reference: a subject known
  only to be in the Other group can be expected to have a *lower* CL than a
  Caucasian one. This is the reading for a label statement or a dosing
  recommendation.
* **Conditional**, `r pick(dfres_scm)` of the reference: a subject of the Other
  group who is otherwise typical can be expected to have a slightly *higher* CL
  than an otherwise identical Caucasian subject. This is the mechanistic reading, and
  the one an SCM Forest plot gives.

Neither number is wrong. They answer different questions, and a plot that does
not say which one it answers invites the reader to take the wrong one.

# 10. Worked example: an SCM model and a FREM model of the same data

On the same data, a Forest plot from a full random effects model (FREM) agrees
with the Forest plot of a model built by stepwise covariate modelling (SCM), for
the covariates in the SCM model, when two conditions hold: the FREM predictions
are fully conditioned, and the FREM plot has the reference subject of the SCM
plot. The differences that remain arise because, in FREM, every covariate has an
effect on every parameter. For a label statement or a dose recommendation, the
recommended FREM plot is unconditional, with a reference per covariate.

## Two models of one data set

PMXForest includes two models of the same simulated data set,
`DAT-1-MI-PMX-2.csv`, in which every dose is oral. Each model comes with a
bootstrap of 175 resamples, run with PsN, and the confidence intervals of the
worked example are computed from the bootstrap.

* **SCM model:** `run7.mod` was built with scmplus, the stepwise covariate
  search of PsN, with stage-wise filtering. In `run7.mod`, weight has effects
  on the clearance `CL` and the volume `V`, and genotype has effects on `CL`
  and on the relative bioavailability `FREL`. Sex and formulation have effects
  on `FREL`, and food has an effect on `CL`.
* **FREM model:** `run22-3.mod` is a FREM model of the data set, built on the
  mechanistic and structural covariates of the SCM model `run7.mod`. In
  `run22-3.mod`, weight, formulation, food and genotype have the fixed effects
  of `run7.mod`, and sex is a FREM covariate instead of a fixed effect on
  `FREL`. The 11 FREM covariates are the data columns `AGE`, `ALT`, `AST`,
  `BILI`, `BMI`, `CRCL`, `ETHNIC`, `HT`, `NCIL`, `RACEL2` and `SEX`, which
  include age, height and creatinine clearance.

Genotype is the 2D6 genotype, with four levels: ultrarapid (2D6 UM), extensive
(2D6 EM), intermediate (2D6 IM) and poor (2D6 PM) metabolisers.

Every plot of the worked example is a plot of the apparent clearance `CL/F`,
which is `CL` divided by `FREL`. After an oral dose, the area under the
concentration curve is the dose divided by `CL/F`, so the exposure of a subject
is inversely proportional to `CL/F`.

```{r we_setup}
simVal <- system.file("extdata/SimVal", package = "PMXForest")
dataWE <- read.csv(file.path(simVal, "DAT-1-MI-PMX-2.csv"))

# the covariates on the rows of the plots
shownWE <- c("WT", "SEX", "FORM", "FOOD", "GENO", "AGE", "CRCL")
# the FREM covariates of run22-3
fremCovsWE <- getCovNames(modFile = file.path(simVal, "run22-3.mod"))$orgCovNames
fremCovsWE

# apparent clearance as a secondary parameter of both models
secondaryWE <- list(CLF = "CL / FREL")

# covRef sets the reference of the genotype indicators GENO1 and GENO3, for
# which the control streams have no reference; the reference of GENO4 is in
# the control streams
genSCM <- createParamFunction(
  file.path(simVal, "run7.mod"),
  parameters = c("FREL", "CL"),
  covRef     = list(GENO1 = 0, GENO3 = 0),
  secondary  = secondaryWE,
  quiet      = TRUE
)
funSCM <- eval(parse(text = paste(genSCM$code, collapse = "\n")))

genFREM <- createFREMParamFunction(
  file.path(simVal, "run22-3.mod"),
  parameters = c("FREL", "CL"),
  covRef     = list(GENO1 = 0, GENO3 = 0),
  secondary  = secondaryWE,
  quiet      = TRUE
)
funFREM <- eval(parse(text = genFREM$code))

# the bootstrap resamples of each model, all 175 of them
samplesSCM <- getSamples(file.path(simVal, "bs7.dir/raw_results_run7bs.csv"),
  extFile = file.path(simVal, "run7.ext")
)
samplesFREM <- getSamples(file.path(simVal, "bs22-3.dir/raw_results_run22-3bs.csv"),
  extFile = file.path(simVal, "run22-3.ext")
)

# row labels, with the names and level names of the PMXForest walkthrough
# vignette
mapsWE <- list(
  name_map = c(
    WT = "Weight", SEX = "Sex", FORM = "Formulation", FOOD = "Food status",
    GENO = "2D6 genotype", AGE = "Age", CRCL = "CRCL"
  ),
  unit_map = c(WT = "kg", AGE = "y", CRCL = "mL/min"),
  level_map = list(
    SEX  = c("1" = "Male", "2" = "Female"),
    FORM = c("0" = "Oral tablet", "1" = "FDC"),
    FOOD = c("0" = "Fasted", "1" = "Fed"),
    GENO = c("1" = "2D6 UM", "2" = "2D6 EM", "3" = "2D6 IM", "4" = "2D6 PM")
  ),
  group_map = c(CRCL = "Creatinine\nclearance")
)
labelWE <- function(dfCovs, dfres) {
  do.call(generateCovNames, c(list(dfCovs, dfres), mapsWE))
}

# the CL/F rows, with a panel name in PARAMETER, for plots side by side
panelWE <- function(dfres, panel) {
  dfres <- dfres[dfres$PARAMETER == "CLF", ]
  dfres$PARAMETER <- panel
  dfres
}

# a logarithmic x axis for the error-bar panels of forestPlot()
logAxisWE <- "scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2))"

# the relative value on one row, as forestPlot() shows it; used for the
# numbers in the text
rel <- function(dfres, row, par) {
  x <- dfres$POINT_NOVAR_REL_REFFUNC[dfres$COVNAME == row & dfres$PARAMETER == par]
  formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
}
```

## The fully conditioned FREM plot agrees with the SCM plot on apparent clearance

A FREM plot can be compared with an SCM plot only when both of two conditions
hold:

* **Fully conditioned predictions:** on each row of the FREM plot, every FREM
  covariate is set to the value of the reference subject, apart from the
  covariate that varies on the row, so that no FREM covariate is integrated
  out. Every FREM covariate is set in this way, not only the covariates on the
  plot. The rows of an SCM plot are conditioned in this way by construction.
  When the other FREM covariates of a row are left missing (at `missVal`), the
  effect on the row is unconditional and includes the effects of the
  covariates that go with the varied covariate in the data.
* **The reference subject of the SCM plot:** a relative value is the
  prediction on a row divided by the prediction for the reference subject, so
  the relative values of two plots with different reference subjects differ
  even where the predictions agree. Without a reference row (`dfRefRow`), the
  reference of a FREM plot is the mean prediction over the data, which is not
  the reference subject of the SCM plot.

In the worked example, the reference subject has the median of each continuous
covariate and the most common level of each categorical covariate. The same
rows (`dfCovs`) and the same reference row (`dfRefRow`) are used for both
models. The rows are built with the covariates in `shownWE` and the FREM
covariates, with `useMissVal = FALSE`, so that every FREM covariate is set on
every row. The rows that vary a FREM covariate outside `shownWE` are then
dropped, to keep the plot short. Each continuous covariate has a row at the 5th
and a row at the 95th percentile of the data, the default of `setupDfCovs()`,
and each categorical covariate has one row per level.

In both models, genotype is coded as the indicators `GENO1`, `GENO3` and
`GENO4`, with level 2 as the reference. With `catRef = list(GENO = 2)`,
`setupDfCovs()` and `setupDfRefRow()` leave out level 2, and with `sep = ""`,
the two functions write the indicator columns without a separator, as `GENO1`
rather than `GENO_1`.

```{r we_conditioned}
allCovsWE <- unique(c(shownWE, fremCovsWE))
dfCovsAllWE <- setupDfCovs(dataWE,
  covariates = allCovsWE, useMissVal = FALSE, idVar = "ID",
  catRef = list(GENO = 2), sep = ""
)
dfCovsWE <- dfCovsAllWE[dfCovsAllWE$COVARIATEGROUPS %in% shownWE, ]
dfRefRowWE <- setupDfRefRow(dfCovsAllWE,
  data = dataWE, covariates = allCovsWE, idVar = "ID",
  catRef = list(GENO = 2), sep = ""
)

dfresSCM <- getForestDFSCM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovsWE,
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRowWE,
  functionList     = list(funSCM),
  functionListName = genSCM$functionListName,
  noBaseThetas     = genSCM$noBaseThetas,
  dfParameters     = samplesSCM,
  quiet            = TRUE
)
dfresSCM <- labelWE(dfCovsWE, dfresSCM)

dfresFREMcond <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovsWE,
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRowWE,
  modName          = "run22-3",
  modDevDir        = simVal,
  dfParameters     = samplesFREM,
  functionList     = list(funFREM),
  functionListName = genFREM$functionListName,
  quiet            = TRUE
)
dfresFREMcond <- labelWE(dfCovsWE, dfresFREMcond)

# one data frame with a panel per model
cols <- intersect(names(dfresSCM), names(dfresFREMcond))
dfresCLF <- rbind(
  panelWE(dfresSCM, "SCM")[cols],
  panelWE(dfresFREMcond, "FREM")[cols]
)
```

In the relative plots of the worked example, the bars are 90% confidence
intervals from the bootstrap. The grey band is the range of relative values
from 0.8 to 1.25. The x axis is logarithmic, so that an effect and the inverse
of the effect, such as 0.5 and 2, are at the same distance from 1.

```{r we_clf_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%"}
forestPlot(dfresCLF,
  parameters = c("SCM", "FREM"),
  xlb = "Relative CL/F",
  rightStrip = FALSE,
  addcodeErr = logAxisWE,
  referenceInfo = "Reference: median of each continuous covariate, most common level of each categorical one"
)
```

For the covariates in the SCM model, the two plots agree. The weight
rows are equal in the two models and have no uncertainty, because the
allometric exponents of weight are fixed in both models. `CL/F` with the
fixed-dose combination (FDC) is `r rel(dfresSCM, "FDC", "CLF")` times `CL/F`
with the oral tablet in the SCM model, and
`r rel(dfresFREMcond, "FDC", "CLF")` times in FREM. `CL/F` of fasted subjects
is `r rel(dfresSCM, "Fasted", "CLF")` times that of fed subjects in the SCM
model, and `r rel(dfresFREMcond, "Fasted", "CLF")` times in FREM. In both
models, genotype has an effect on `CL`, and the poor metaboliser genotype has
an effect on `FREL` as well. `CL/F` of poor metabolisers is
`r rel(dfresSCM, "2D6 PM", "CLF")` times that of extensive metabolisers in the
SCM model, and `r rel(dfresFREMcond, "2D6 PM", "CLF")` times in FREM.

In the SCM model, sex has an effect on `FREL` alone, while in FREM, sex has an
effect on every parameter. `CL/F` of females is
`r rel(dfresSCM, "Female", "CLF")` times that of males in the SCM model, and
`r rel(dfresFREMcond, "Female", "CLF")` times in FREM, with overlapping
confidence intervals. Age and creatinine clearance are not in the SCM model, so
every row of the two covariates is at 1 in the SCM plot. In FREM, age and
creatinine clearance have effects on `CL/F` as well, but the effects are close
to 1, and the confidence intervals include 1. In an SCM, only the effects that
pass the selection are kept in the model, so small effects of this size are
left out.

## Without a reference row, the reference of a FREM plot lies between the levels of a categorical covariate

In the default FREM plot, the predictions are unconditional and no reference
row is given. On each row, only the covariate that varies on the row is set,
and the other FREM covariates are integrated out over the data. The reference
is the prediction with every FREM covariate integrated out, which is the mean
prediction over the population. For a categorical FREM covariate, the reference
is therefore a mix of the levels and lies between them, so no level of the
covariate is at 1. A categorical covariate without a level at 1 is often found
hard to understand.

With a reference per covariate, each covariate is compared with the median or
the most common level of the same covariate, and the other FREM covariates are
integrated out in the reference as on the rows. The reference per covariate is
set with `singleRef = FALSE` in `setupDfRefRow()`. On the relative scale, the
reference level of each categorical covariate is then at 1, as in an SCM plot,
so that the plot is less surprising to read.

```{r we_unconditional}
# unconditional rows: one covariate set per row, the others missing
dfCovsUncondWE <- setupDfCovs(dataWE,
  covariates = shownWE, idVar = "ID",
  catRef = list(GENO = 2), sep = ""
)

# the FREM default, without dfRefRow
dfresFREMdefault <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovsUncondWE,
  modName          = "run22-3",
  modDevDir        = simVal,
  dfParameters     = samplesFREM,
  functionList     = list(funFREM),
  functionListName = genFREM$functionListName,
  quiet            = TRUE
)
dfresFREMdefault <- labelWE(dfCovsUncondWE, dfresFREMdefault)

# a reference per covariate: in each reference row, the covariate of the
# row is at the median or the most common level, and the others are missing
dfRefRowVaryingWE <- setupDfRefRow(dfCovsUncondWE,
  data = dataWE, covariates = shownWE, singleRef = FALSE, idVar = "ID",
  catRef = list(GENO = 2), sep = ""
)
dfresFREMuncond <- getForestDFFREM(
  dfCovs           = dfCovsUncondWE,
  dfRefRow         = dfRefRowVaryingWE,
  modName          = "run22-3",
  modDevDir        = simVal,
  dfParameters     = samplesFREM,
  functionList     = list(funFREM),
  functionListName = genFREM$functionListName,
  quiet            = TRUE
)
dfresFREMuncond <- labelWE(dfCovsUncondWE, dfresFREMuncond)

# one data frame with a panel per reference
cols <- intersect(names(dfresFREMdefault), names(dfresFREMuncond))
dfresRefWE <- rbind(
  panelWE(dfresFREMdefault, "No reference row")[cols],
  panelWE(dfresFREMuncond, "Reference per covariate")[cols]
)

# the number of subjects with each formulation, one record per subject
baseWE <- dataWE[!duplicated(dataWE$ID), ]
table(baseWE$FORM)
```

```{r we_reference_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%"}
forestPlot(dfresRefWE,
  parameters = c("No reference row", "Reference per covariate"),
  xlb = "Relative CL/F",
  statisticsLabel = "",
  rightStrip = FALSE,
  errbartabwidth = c(2, 1.3, 2, 1.3),
  addcodeErr = logAxisWE,
  referenceInfo = "Unconditional effects, without a reference row and with a reference per covariate"
)
```

Without a reference row, `CL/F` of males is
`r rel(dfresFREMdefault, "Male", "CLF")` times the reference, and `CL/F` of
females is `r rel(dfresFREMdefault, "Female", "CLF")` times the reference. With
a reference per covariate, males are at 1, and `CL/F` of females is
`r rel(dfresFREMuncond, "Female", "CLF")` times that of males.

Weight, formulation, food and genotype are not FREM covariates in
`run22-3.mod`. When one of the four covariates is missing, on a row or in a
reference, the parameter function puts the covariate at the reference of the
model, which is the value at which the covariate effect in the control stream
is 1. The reference of the model is 75 kg for weight, the FDC for formulation,
fed for food and the extensive metaboliser genotype. In the panel without a
reference row, these values are the reference of the plot. In the panel with a
reference per covariate, the reference of each covariate is the median or the
most common level in the data. For food and genotype, the two references are
the same level, which is at 1 in both panels. For weight and formulation, the
two references differ. The median weight in the data is `r dfRefRowWE$WT` kg.
The most common formulation in the data is the oral tablet, with
`r sum(baseWE$FORM == 0)` of `r nrow(baseWE)` subjects.

## The recommended FREM plot is unconditional, with a reference per covariate

The unconditional effect of a covariate is the effect to expect in a subject
known only by that covariate, which is the effect that a label statement or a
dose recommendation is about. With a reference per covariate, the reference
level of each categorical covariate is at 1 on the relative scale, as in an SCM
plot, while the effects stay unconditional. The unconditional plot with a
reference per covariate is therefore the recommended way to present a FREM-based
Forest plot.

```{r we_height}
# mean height of males and females in the data, one record per subject
heightWE <- round(tapply(baseWE$HT, baseWE$SEX, mean))
heightWE
```

In the unconditional plot with a reference per covariate, `CL/F` of females is
`r rel(dfresFREMuncond, "Female", "CLF")` times that of males, against
`r rel(dfresFREMcond, "Female", "CLF")` in the fully conditioned FREM plot. In
the data, females are shorter than males on average, at `r heightWE[["2"]]`
against `r heightWE[["1"]]` cm, and height is a FREM covariate. The
unconditional effect of sex includes the effect of a difference in height,
while in the fully conditioned plot, height is held at the reference.

On the absolute scale, the reference of each covariate can be seen. Each
covariate has a reference line, at the predicted `CL/F` for the reference
subject of the covariate. The grey band around each line is the range from 0.8
to 1.25 times the reference.

```{r we_absolute_plot, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 7, out.width = "100%"}
forestPlot(dfresFREMuncond,
  parameters = "CLF",
  parameterLabels = "CL/F",
  plotRelative = FALSE,
  sigdigits = 3,
  xlb = "CL/F",
  rightStrip = FALSE,
  addcodeErr = "scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50))",
  referenceInfo = "Reference per covariate: the median or most common level of each"
)
```

The reference lines are at different values of `CL/F`, because the reference
subject differs between covariates. The reference subject of each covariate has
the median or the most common level of that covariate, and every other
covariate is missing. The other FREM covariates are therefore integrated out,
and weight, formulation, food and genotype are at the reference of the model.
The reference subject for weight weighs `r dfRefRowWE$WT` kg, and the reference
subjects for the other covariates weigh 75 kg.

## compareFREMSCM() builds the comparison in one call

`compareFREMSCM()` builds a comparison of the two models in one call, with one
plot per parameter. The rows of a parameter hold the covariates that the SCM
model has on that parameter, and the FREM predictions are integrated over the
other FREM covariates, as the predictions of the SCM model are by leaving those
covariates out. On `CL/F`, which is `CL` divided by `FREL`, the rows therefore
hold weight, sex, formulation, food and genotype, the covariates of `CL` and of
`FREL` together. Sex is the one FREM covariate among them, so the FREM
predictions are integrated over the other ten FREM covariates, including height.
The function gives both models one reference subject, passes genotype to each
model in the coding the model reads, and draws the two plots side by side. The
function also returns a table of the effects of both models, a text that
describes the differences, and a figure legend. The labels are those of the
worked example, in `mapsWE`.

```{r we_compare, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, out.width = "100%"}
resWE <- do.call(compareFREMSCM, c(
  list(
    scmModel        = file.path(simVal, "run7.mod"),
    fremModel       = file.path(simVal, "run22-3.mod"),
    data            = dataWE,
    parameters      = c("FREL", "CL"),
    secondary       = secondaryWE,
    plotParameters  = "CLF",
    parameterLabels = c(CLF = "CL/F"),
    samplesSCM      = file.path(simVal, "bs7.dir/raw_results_run7bs.csv"),
    samplesFREM     = file.path(simVal, "bs22-3.dir/raw_results_run22-3bs.csv")
  ),
  mapsWE
))
resWE
```

The SCM values are those of the plots above, because the SCM model reads none
of the FREM covariates other than sex. In FREM, `CL/F` of females is
`r rel(resWE$dfres[resWE$dfres$MODEL == "FREM", ], "Female", "CLF")` times that
of males, against `r rel(resWE$dfres[resWE$dfres$MODEL == "SCM", ], "Female", "CLF")`
in the SCM model and `r rel(dfresFREMcond, "Female", "CLF")` in the fully
conditioned FREM plot. In the fully conditioned plot, height and the other FREM
covariates are held at the reference. Here, the FREM predictions are integrated
over them, as the predictions of the SCM model are. The text and the legend are
printed with
`print(resWE, text = TRUE)`, or read from the result. No verdict on the
agreement of the two models is given in the text: the rows are counted by the
direction of the two effects relative to 1, and each row is described with the
two point estimates.

```{r we_compare_text}
writeLines(resWE$description)
writeLines(strwrap(resWE$legend))
```
